lessonTitle: Sterilisation and Disinfection: Autoclaving, Chemical Agents and Choosing a Method

blocks.text: A tray of surgical instruments is wrapped, loaded into a steam steriliser and run for a standard cycle. A strip on the pack changes colour, yet the theatre team still waits for the biological indicator before trusting the load. Why is a boiled kettle not good enough, and why does one rare bacterial form decide how the whole process is designed?

blocks.markdown: Preventing the transfer of microorganisms on instruments, surfaces and skin needs a clear vocabulary and a logical choice of method. The correct method depends on what has to be removed, where the item has been, and what damage it can tolerate.

blocks.title: Sterilisation, disinfection and antisepsis
blocks.text: Sterilisation is the complete destruction or removal of all viable microorganisms, including bacterial spores. Disinfection is the reduction of microorganisms on inanimate objects to a level that is not harmful; it does not necessarily destroy spores. Antisepsis is the application of a chemical agent to living tissue (skin or mucous membrane) to reduce microorganisms. Cleaning, the physical removal of organic material, must precede all three, because soil protects microbes and neutralises many agents.

blocks.caption: Comparison of the three terms
rows: Hypochlorite on a surface; glutaraldehyde for an endoscope
Chlorhexidine or alcohol on skin before incision

blocks.markdown: **Why spores matter.** Bacterial endospores (for example *Bacillus* and *Clostridium* species) have a thick protein coat, a dehydrated core and calcium dipicolinate that make them extraordinarily resistant to heat, drying and many chemicals. A process that kills them will kill everything else, so sterilisation processes are validated using spores, such as *Geobacillus stearothermophilus* for steam.

**Autoclaving (moist heat under pressure).** An autoclave uses saturated steam in a sealed chamber. Raising the pressure raises the boiling point of water, so steam temperature reaches 121 degrees Celsius at about 103 kPa above atmospheric pressure (15 psi), usually held for **15 minutes**, or 134 degrees Celsius at about 206 kPa (30 psi) for about **3 minutes**. Steam kills by **denaturing proteins and enzymes** and disrupting structures; moist heat is far more efficient than dry heat because steam condenses on the cooler items and releases latent heat directly into them, and water allows protein denaturation at lower temperatures. All the **air must be removed** from the chamber and the load, since trapped air lowers the temperature reached and prevents steam contact. A sterilisation cycle is checked by physical gauges, **chemical indicators** (colour change) and **biological indicators** (spore strips that must not grow after the cycle). Dry heat (hot air oven) needs a much longer time, for example 160 degrees Celsius for two hours, and is used for glassware, powders and oils.

blocks.caption: D: decimal reduction time (time to kill 90% of the organisms at a fixed temperature); N0: initial number; N: final number; t: exposure time

blocks.title: Time to reduce a spore load
blocks.prompt: A load carries 10^6 spores with a D-value of 1.5 minutes at the cycle temperature. How long is needed to reduce the expected survivors to 10^-6 (one in a million)?

steps.text: Required log reduction = log10(10^6 / 10^-6) = log10(10^12) = 12 log units.
Time = D x log reduction = 1.5 min x 12 = 18 minutes.

blocks.markdown: **Other methods.** **Low-temperature methods** (ethylene oxide gas, hydrogen peroxide plasma) sterilise heat-sensitive items but need aeration or specialised equipment. **Filtration** removes organisms from heat-labile fluids. **Ionising radiation** is used for single-use medical products. **Chemical disinfectants**: alcohol (about 70%, rapid, not sporicidal, a skin antiseptic and for clean surfaces); chlorhexidine (antiseptic, poor against spores); povidone-iodine (antiseptic); sodium hypochlorite (broad spectrum including spores at sufficient concentration; corrosive); glutaraldehyde and peracetic acid (high-level disinfection of heat-sensitive equipment, and sporicidal with enough contact time).

**Choosing a method: the Spaulding classification.** Items are grouped by the risk of infection if contaminated. **Critical** items enter sterile tissue or the bloodstream (surgical instruments, implants, needles) and must be **sterile**. **Semi-critical** items contact intact mucous membranes or non-intact skin (flexible endoscopes, respiratory equipment) and need at least **high-level disinfection**, ideally sterilisation if possible. **Non-critical** items touch only intact skin (blood pressure cuff, stethoscope, bed rails) and need **cleaning with low- or intermediate-level disinfection**.

blocks.caption: Spaulding classification and appropriate decontamination
rows: Surgical instruments, implants, urinary catheters on insertion

blocks.title: Choosing for a given item
blocks.prompt: (a) A reusable heat-tolerant surgical forceps; (b) a heat-sensitive flexible bronchoscope; (c) a patient's bed rail. Choose a decontamination approach for each.

steps.text: (a) Critical item, tolerates heat: steam sterilisation (autoclave) after cleaning.
(b) Semi-critical, heat-sensitive: thorough cleaning followed by high-level disinfection (such as peracetic acid or glutaraldehyde) or low-temperature sterilisation.
(c) Non-critical: cleaning with detergent and a surface disinfectant.

blocks.answer: (a) Autoclave; (b) clean plus high-level disinfection; (c) clean and low-level disinfect.

blocks.title: Match risk to process
blocks.text: The higher the risk of the item's contact site, the higher the level of microbial kill required, and the process must be able to kill spores whenever sterility is required.

blocks.title: Pitfalls
blocks.text: Alcohol does not kill spores and is inactivated by organic material. Boiling water does not sterilise. Wrapped packs with trapped air can fail in an autoclave despite reaching the set time.

points: Sterilisation kills all organisms including spores; disinfection reduces organisms on inanimate objects; antisepsis applies to living tissue.
Autoclaving uses pressurised steam (121 degrees Celsius for 15 minutes or 134 degrees Celsius for about 3 minutes) to denature proteins and kill spores.
The Spaulding classification (critical, semi-critical, non-critical) guides the method chosen for each item.

questions.stem: Which term describes the application of a chemical agent to living skin to reduce the number of microorganisms?

distractorRationale.b: Sterilisation destroys all organisms and is not applied to living tissue.
distractorRationale.c: Disinfection is used on inanimate objects.
distractorRationale.d: Autoclaving would damage tissue and is for equipment.

questions.explanation: Antisepsis is the reduction of microbes on living tissue with agents such as chlorhexidine or alcohol. Sterilisation and disinfection apply to inanimate objects.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes sterilisation from disinfection?

options.text: Sterilisation destroys all microorganisms including spores; disinfection reduces numbers and may not kill spores
Sterilisation is used on skin; disinfection on instruments
Disinfection is always more effective than sterilisation

questions.correctOptionText: Sterilisation destroys all microorganisms including spores; disinfection reduces numbers and may not kill spores

distractorRationale.b: Skin treatment is antisepsis, not sterilisation.
distractorRationale.d: Disinfection is a lower level of microbial kill.

questions.explanation: Sterilisation is an absolute concept: all viable organisms, including spores, are destroyed. Disinfection is a reduction to a safe level, usually without sporicidal activity.

questions.stem: What is the principal mechanism by which moist heat in an autoclave kills bacterial spores?

distractorRationale.b: Spores of Gram-positive bacteria have no LPS layer.
distractorRationale.d: Ionising damage describes irradiation, not steam.

questions.explanation: Pressurised steam transfers heat efficiently and denatures essential proteins. This is why moist heat is more effective than dry heat at the same temperature.

questions.stem: Why must air be removed from an autoclave chamber and from wrapped loads before the cycle timing begins?

options.text: Trapped air lowers the temperature reached and prevents steam contacting the items
Air reacts with steam to form a toxic gas
Air raises the boiling point of water above 134 degrees Celsius
Air has no effect on sterilisation

questions.correctOptionText: Trapped air lowers the temperature reached and prevents steam contacting the items

distractorRationale.c: Air does not change the boiling point in this way; pressure raises it.
distractorRationale.d: Air pockets are a common cause of failed cycles.

questions.explanation: Sterilisation relies on saturated steam condensing on the items. Air pockets insulate surfaces and lower the temperature there, leaving organisms alive.

questions.stem: A reusable flexible gastroscope, which is heat-sensitive and contacts intact mucous membranes, has just been used. After thorough manual cleaning, what is the minimum appropriate further decontamination?

options.text: High-level disinfection with a suitable chemical agent

questions.correctOptionText: High-level disinfection with a suitable chemical agent

distractorRationale.b: Alcohol wiping is inadequate for an endoscope channel.
distractorRationale.d: Cleaning alone does not reach the required microbial reduction.

questions.explanation: Items that contact mucous membranes are semi-critical and need at least high-level disinfection after cleaning. Heat-sensitive devices cannot be autoclaved.

questions.stem: A load carries 10^5 spores with a D-value of 2.0 minutes at the cycle temperature. Using t = D x log10(N0/N), calculate the exposure time needed to reduce the expected number of survivors to 10^-4. Give the time in minutes.
questions.explanation: The log reduction is log10(10^5 / 10^-4) = log10(10^9) = 9. The time is 2.0 x 9 = 18 minutes.

questions.stem: A ward needs 2.0 litres of surface disinfectant at 1 000 ppm available chlorine, to be made from a stock hypochlorite solution of 50 000 ppm. Using C1V1 = C2V2, calculate the volume of stock needed in millilitres.
questions.explanation: V1 = C2 x V2 / C1 = 1000 x 2000 mL / 50 000 = 40 mL of stock, made up to 2.0 litres with water. Correct dilution matters because too weak a solution fails to disinfect and too strong damages surfaces.

questions.stem: Define sterilisation, disinfection and antisepsis, and give one example of each.
markingGuide: Sterilisation: complete destruction of all viable organisms including spores (autoclave, ethylene oxide)
Disinfection: reduction of organisms on inanimate objects to a safe level, not necessarily killing spores (hypochlorite, glutaraldehyde)
Antisepsis: reduction of organisms on living tissue (chlorhexidine, alcohol, povidone-iodine)
questions.explanation: Each term differs by target and by the degree of kill. Cleaning first is essential because organic soil protects microorganisms.

questions.stem: Describe how an autoclave sterilises equipment and why spores are used to monitor its performance.
markingGuide: Saturated steam under pressure raises temperature (121 degrees Celsius for 15 min or 134 degrees Celsius for about 3 min)
Steam condenses on items releasing latent heat and denatures proteins and enzymes
Air removal needed so steam contacts all surfaces
Spores are the most heat-resistant forms (protein coat, dehydrated core, dipicolinic acid)
Biological indicators (for example Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores) confirm lethality; chemical indicators and gauges are also used
questions.explanation: Pressure raises the temperature of steam, which then transfers heat efficiently. Spores are used as indicators because if they are killed, less resistant organisms are also killed.

questions.stem: Using the Spaulding classification, select and justify a decontamination method for each of: a heat-tolerant instrument set for a hernia repair, a heat-sensitive reusable cystoscope, and a stethoscope.
markingGuide: Hernia instrument set: critical item entering sterile tissue; sterilisation (autoclave) after cleaning

Cystoscope: contacts mucosa (semi-critical, though it passes into a normally sterile tract so sterilisation is preferred where possible) and is heat-sensitive; cleaning then high-level disinfection or low-temperature sterilisation
Stethoscope: non-critical, intact skin only; cleaning with low-level disinfection
Justification based on risk of infection and tolerance to heat
questions.explanation: The risk category of the contact site determines the minimum level of decontamination. Heat tolerance then decides which method can be used at that level.
